title: The Pension Administration Gap: What’s Blocking the Industry
summary: See how AI and modern pension administration can help insurers overcome legacy system limitations and scale PRT opportunities.
body_markdown:
The challenges insurers face in tapping into the growing pension risk transfer (PRT) market can begin, metaphorically speaking, at the front door. When a broker representing a pension plan sponsor puts out a request for proposals (RFP), it immediately creates a long to-do list. The carrier must:


- Ingest all plan details, including all variations on benefit options, assessing installation needs


- Capture detailed demographics for all participants
- Assess the ability to support the plan within the carrier’s current policy administration system
- Determine development time and resources needed to upgrade if the current PAS or other capabilities fall short


This is often a time-consuming, labor-intensive series of workstreams that can hamstring an insurer’s ability to compete for additional opportunities as they arise. The question may become whether the carrier is willing and able to add headcount and resources to increase bandwidth and entertain more opportunities. For many, the issue is not only efficiency; it is whether they can bid at all. Often the deciding factors are the carrier’s capabilities and its capacity to install a case once it is won, rather than how quickly an RFP can be assessed. When either falls short, an insurer may simply decline to bid, and competing priorities with the onboarding team only add to the strain.


AI, however, is opening new avenues to meet this challenge. An AI agent can increasingly help assess the carrier’s capabilities against the plan’s requirements to determine feasibility, including whether it makes sense to go further into the bid process and what the insurer can accommodate. With that finding, AI can help configure the plan and options to accelerate not only the response to an RFP but also the installation that follows, so the insurer can move on to the next opportunity. Because PRT still involves a great deal of judgment, the most realistic approach keeps a human in the loop: AI does the heavy lifting of interpreting requirements and preparing configurations, while experienced people review, validate, and make the final call.


That work shouldn’t stop when the bid is submitted. The plan information and requirements gathered during bidding should carry directly into onboarding, rather than having to be recreated once a case is won. When bidding and installation are connected this way, the effort invested up front becomes a head start on implementation.


This dynamic can help carriers of all sizes. A large carrier can now bid on complex, jumbo deals without exhaustive manual support, while those at the smaller end of the market can pursue many more transactions. Capacity matters here beyond efficiency: many providers may look at a potential deal and not bid at all because they lack the capabilities or installation capacity to support it. By assessing opportunities faster and reducing the effort required to install each case, the combination of AI and a FAST PRT solution can expand an insurer’s addressable market, bringing deals within reach that might otherwise have been passed over. It is also not only about supporting today’s plans and options, but about being able to grow, scale, and accommodate new variations in plan and benefit options.


## Next step: onboarding


When a transaction is won, there’s still more work ahead that can be either slow and manual or quick and automated. Slow onboarding of contracts is often intertwined with manual workflows. Onboarding timelines are generally well defined, and participant information and circumstances will change along the way regardless of how fast a case moves. The opportunity is to help insurers manage those changes more efficiently, through bulk loads, reporting, and similar automation, rather than restarting work each time something changes.


Why are there so many manual processes? The issue often traces to outdated legacy systems, which may be siloed and connected piecemeal, requiring human intervention to complete handoffs from one tool to the next.


Legacy systems may depend on data that customers, brokers, or an insurer’s own staff enter manually. These processes can be slow and error-prone, requiring review and more rework to correct mistakes.


There is a strong story in combining AI with a configurable policy administration system such as FAST. AI can help interpret requirements, identify data issues, and automate workflows, but insurers still need a platform flexible enough to administer complex transactions. It is the combination that helps insurers take on more, and increasingly complex, business.


## Setting up long-term success


Meanwhile, customers’, consultants’, and brokers’ expectations are outrunning what many insurers can deliver. The same fast turnaround and digital self-service options that have become table stakes across many industries are now coming to pension providers. Meeting those demands will require many insurers to finally confront the drag of fragmented legacy workflows.


Modernization isn’t simply about replacing outdated technology or replicating existing functionality on a new platform. It’s about designing systems with the agility, flexibility, and scalability to support both existing and new products, adapt to evolving business requirements, and accommodate future growth. In many cases, carriers are not looking to replace legacy administration systems because they cannot support existing products. Rather, these systems often lack the flexibility and scalability needed to efficiently onboard and administer new products. As the PRT market continues to evolve, modernization must go beyond replacing outdated technology. Solutions like FAST, with its configurable and scalable architecture, show how modern administration platforms can adapt to changing business requirements without extensive customization or manual intervention. Combined with AI, they can reduce the effort required to install each case and increase installation capacity, even when key dates such as first payment and certificate release are already set.


What’s at stake is more than just pleasing customers with speed and convenience; a pension is often the participant’s livelihood, covering the bills. Accurate, on-time benefit payments are table stakes for any mature policy administration system, and participants and plan sponsors rightly expect them. Modern platforms continue to strengthen that reliability, to the point where insurers no longer need to think about check runs.
